title: An atom's weight
hook: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it (Quran 99:7–8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a short line from the Quran: every soul will taste of death. Your line was every soul. Did you say it to anyone in traffic? That verse pointed past death to a day of accounting. Today, how small the accounting gets. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

The ground moves. That's how the ninety-ninth surah of the Quran begins, the one called the Earthquake. The earth is shaken, and it throws up what it has been carrying. A person looks at it and asks: what is the matter with her? And on that day, the surah says, the earth tells her news. Then people come out in scattered groups to be shown what they did. And the surah ends with two lines so short and so balanced they're easy to carry: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of ill will see it.
screen: `THE GROUND MOVES.` → `THE EARTH TELLS ITS NEWS.` → `PEOPLE ARE SHOWN WHAT THEY DID.`

segments.voice: First, the earth speaks. In this surah, the ground itself is a witness. The floor you walked on, the street you crossed, has been listening, and on that day it tells what happened on it. It's a strange and striking picture: nothing done anywhere goes unrecorded. Second, an atom's weight. Pickthall's translation reads: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." The Arabic phrase is mithqala dharratin, the weight of a dharra, something tiny. Pickthall chose atom. Some readers picture a small ant, or a speck of dust floating in a sunbeam. Either way, it's the smallest thing you can still name. Third, both directions. The two verses mirror each other. Small harms count: the sharp word, the little lie. But small goods count just as surely: the held door, the returned text. For Muslims, nothing is too small to be seen by God. Fourth, don't belittle it. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells a companion not to look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. Put next to this surah, the point is easy to hear. The great question of death, judgment and what comes after is answered here in the smallest unit there is. Not a grand gesture. An atom's weight, done today, on ground that remembers.
screen: `THE GROUND IS A WITNESS.` · `THE WEIGHT OF SOMETHING TINY.` · `SMALL GOOD AND SMALL ILL BOTH COUNT.` · `DON'T BELITTLE A KIND FACE.` · then, large: `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Then let your mind go over the next few hours. Somewhere in them there's a small good waiting, so small it would be easy to skip: a message to someone who's alone, a dish washed that isn't yours, a cheerful face for a tired cashier. Pick one. Just one, and keep it small. Picture yourself doing it, and let the breath stay easy. If you pray, you can offer the small deed to God before you do it. After the bell, go and do it. The bell holds the time.
Dharra, the Arabic word for something tiny, the Quran's picture of the smallest deed, good or ill, that every person will see. Today's word.
Your line: ground that remembers. Today, do the one small good you chose, and don't tell anyone about it. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Surah az-Zalzalah is short, and some Muslims recite it in daily prayer; Muslims recall its last two verses as a reason not to belittle small good deeds or small wrongs.

original.note: Arabic, Quran 99:7–8: the weight of a tiny thing, an atom's weight.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scary warning that God is watching your every mistake.
what it means: good and ill, even the smallest, will be seen; small goods count too.
what a scholar hears: dharra names something tiny; Pickthall chose atom, and some readers picture a small ant or a speck of dust.
